items.title: Frank Turek Fights ‘War on Reality,’ Offers Warning for America
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "Dystopia"
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Apologist Frank Turek is on a mission to tackle the “war on reality,” warning Americans face a “dystopia” if the nation continues marching toward Marxism.

Turek’s new book, “The War on Reality Workbook: Recovering Truth in a World That Celebrates Lies,” is being released as the nation recently remembered the one-year anniversary of the assassination of conservative and Christian commentator Charlie Kirk.

The apologist told CBN News he and his coauthor, Phoenix Hayes, dedicated the book to Kirk, calling the late Turning Point USA founder a “warrior for reality.”

Turek broke down the current state of culture and decried many elements that simply make no logical — or biblical — sense.

“Abortion is healthcare; we’re pulling baby body parts out of women, and we’re calling that health care,” he said. “That’s a war on reality, and Charlie was a casualty in the war on reality. But, thankfully, since he was a believer, all the murderer was able to do is change his address.”

Turek continued, “He’s absent from the body, present with the Lord, and we remain behind, still engaged in fighting for reality when so many forces are fighting against.”

items.title: Christian Singer Colton Dixon Says Charlie Kirk’s Assassination ‘Changed’ Him
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "It gave me a new outlook on things."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Christian singer-songwriter Colton Dixon said the assassination of Charlie Kirk and the government’s restrictive response to the COVID-19 pandemic “changed” him.

Dixon, 35, told CBN News seeing Kirk murdered for exercising his right to free speech pushed him “to seek truth harder.”

“I feel like, just for a lot of people, whether you believed in what Charlie stood for or not, just for a lot of people, it was, like, it just — I don’t know, it changed me,” said Dixon. “It was just, like, ‘Wow.’ [It] gave me a new outlook on things, even just to seek truth harder.”

The up-and-coming generation, he added, aren’t taking things at face-value anymore, regardless of the source. “They’re seeking truth for themselves,” he explained.

As a Christian recording artist, Dixon said he believes he has found the answer: “The answer’s Jesus.”

The recent spate of culture-defining events have, according to the “Build a Boat” singer, “anchored my feet down in my beliefs so that I’m not going to be pushed around by a little Chihuahua who might bark louder.”

“I kind of even really figured out why I believe what I believe,” he said. “[B]ecause again, it’s just COVID and just all these different things, they’re trying to get you to do different things and I’m like, ‘OK, why aren’t we just going to do it?’ Let’s figure out why so we’re not just being stubborn [and] hardheaded.”

“We open up God’s Word, we pray, we seek godly wisdom, and then we come to the conclusion, ‘Oh, this is why,'” Dixon said. “So now I just feel more steadfast in why I believe what I believe.”

As he’s ruminated on his convictions in recent years, Dixon has become noticeably more comfortable creating edgier content — at least edgier for the status quo in the contemporary Christian music world.

The “American Idol” alumnus just released a new song, “Bones,” based on the Old Testament passage of Ezekiel 37, chronicling the story of the prophet being transported to a valley filled with dry bones. God asked whether the bones could live and then commanded Ezekiel to prophesy over them. As the prophet began speaking promises to the bones, they assembled and were covered in flesh. Then a second prophecy called breath to fill their lungs and they became a living army standing to their feet.

Dixon said the song is “straight from Scripture,” recalling reading the biblical account and feeling “super inspired” and “like God gave me revelation” about speaking “over the dead things in your life.”

During a time of year when most of American culture is fixated on death from a secular perspective, Dixon saw an opportunity to flip the script around Halloween with a biblical understanding of death.

“What if we could … take this passage that already theatrically lines up with a lot of the visuals of skeletons — that’s what this whole passage was, it was a valley of dry bones, the bones rattling, coming together, flesh coming upon the bones, it was like zombies out there, you know, in Ezekiel 37,” he reflected.

That passage of Scripture, Dixon emphasized, shows a biblical interpretation of death, which, for the Christian, he said, is “just a little blip on the timeline of what our lives look like.”

He said, “For the rest of the world, death is the final word. … That’s the period. Life after death is this big mystery. But for a believer, death is not the final word; the cross —what Jesus did on the cross — is the final word, and not only that, but three days later, Him resurrecting from the grave so that we could spend eternal life with Him in heaven. … Death can be a scary thing to talk about, but as a believer, I don’t think it should be.”

The song — and its music video, which is set at night in a graveyard — is certainly unorthodox in its approach, but it paints a clear picture to the world that this life is not all there is. It also tells the story of spiritual power, a nod toward Romans 8:11, where Paul wrote, “The Spirit of God, who raised Jesus from the dead, lives in you. And just as God raised Christ Jesus from the dead, he will give life to your mortal bodies by this same Spirit living within you” (NLT).

“I think that this song is … a kick in the pants for sideline Christians, where I’ve found myself before,” said Dixon. “It’s time to start using the spiritual authority that we have as believers and not just talk the talk, but walk it, as well.”

In fact, for Dixon, it was his wife Annie’s certainty about spiritual authority that led him to do some self-reflection.

“I found myself being so in awe of [my wife] that that was her first response [to pray and speak over things],” he said. “But then also going, ‘Why isn’t that mine?’ You know? If I’m really going to be the best spiritual leader of our house, I need to stop kicking my feet up and actually get in the game and start doing this for real.”

items.title: Bring Your Bible and Your Shotgun: Meet the Most Florida Church Plant Ever
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: Sunday services at TruLife Church of Ocala’s newest campus come with a soundtrack of shotguns going off in the distance. Some attendees bring their own and check them at a rack by the door, the way other congregations check strollers. The campus is called BlackJack, like the range it meets at: Black
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Sunday services at TruLife Church of Ocala’s newest campus come with a soundtrack of shotguns going off in the distance. Some attendees bring their own and check them at a rack by the door, the way other congregations check strollers.

The campus is called BlackJack, like the range it meets at: Blackjack Sporting Clays, a shooting facility in Sumterville, Fla. The facility’s owners came up with the idea and asked pastor Michael Kirby about starting a church plant on the property. Kirby has a handy comparison for the place, which has four courses and a cart. “You rent a golf cart and you drive around and shoot clays at all the different posts,” he said. “It’s like playing golf, but you’re playing with a shotgun.” So it’s golf, but the clubs go off.

The sanctuary, loosely speaking, is a pavilion enclosed in thick, clear plastic, with mobile air conditioners keeping the cool air in and the wooded views visible. An 80-inch TV and a full sound system play Kirby’s prerecorded sermon three weeks a month, so three Sundays out of four the preacher arrives by screen. He or another TruLife pastor preaches live once a month, and Kirby’s daughter-in-law, Taylor Kirby, leads worship. Seating is about 40.

The church held a soft opening a couple of months ago and had its official launch on Sunday, Oct. 25, with Kirby preaching and a picnic lunch afterward. The day before, during a national competitive shooting event at the facility, volunteers handed out flyers and went door to door in the neighborhood, which is outreach with an unusually loud backdrop.

The target audience is the person who came to shoot. “We are hoping to attract unchurched people who are coming to BlackJack to do some shooting,” Kirby said. “Maybe they wouldn’t want to go to your typical church, but they decide they could go over here under the pavilion and hang out.” Evangelism by proximity, in other words: set up next to the people with the shotguns and hope they wander over.

Some of them already have noticed the music. Kirby says shooters have told him they can hear the worship from the service, and he is counting on it. “They might not come inside yet, but they’ll be out there worshipping in the middle of the grass,” he said. The worship set, it turns out, doubles as the range’s ambient soundtrack.

items.title: Yes, Cardinal Vesco, We Are Called to Convert the World
items.author: Dr. Tod Worner
items.summary:
Dr. Tod Worner

Curiously, there seems to be a violent allergy, including among Catholics, to the word “convert.”
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Tod Worner

One of the two who heard John speak and followed him was Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother. He first found his brother Simon and said to him, “We have found the Messiah.” He brought Simon to Jesus. 

—John 1:40-42

Philip found Nathanael and said to him, “We have found him about whom Moses in the law and also the prophets wrote, Jesus son of Joseph from Nazareth.” Nathanael said to him, “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” Philip said to him, “Come and see.”

—John 1:45-46

Jesus said to him, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.”

—John 14:6

Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything that I have commanded you.

—Matt 28: 19-20

To convert or not to convert, that is the question. 

In recent days, Algerian Cardinal Jean-Paul Vesco held a brief interview with journalist Christophe Herinckx from CathoBel, the French-language Catholic multimedia network in Belgium. Ostensibly, the warm exchange was about the state of Catholicism in Algeria, Pope Leo XIV’s visit, and the virtues of synodality. But it was the conversation about inter-religious relations that stirred up criticism surrounding Cardinal Vesco’s opinion on the evangelizing mission of the Catholic Church. “We are the Church of the people,” the Cardinal noted, “Not a proselytizing Church, not a Church that is there to convert, but a Church that aspires to be one of the constituent parts of this people.” 

Bishop Robert Barron called Cardinal Vesco’s assertion “puzzling.” Reasonably perplexed that a Prince of the Church might be confused regarding the raison d’être of Christ’s institution on earth, Bishop reminded, 

The entire thrust of the Second Vatican Council was toward bringing the Light of Christ to the peoples of the world (Lumen Gentium). And this missionary élan has given rise in the last few decades to the idea of a “new evangelization,” which is to say, a fresh declaration of the Lordship of Christ. Quite obviously, no one thinks that this work of evangelization should be done in a brow-beating, overbearing, or disrespectful manner (proselytization), but for God’s sake, let’s not throw the baby out with the bathwater. If I really thought that the Church does not exist to bring people to Christ, then I would resign and get an honest job.

Cardinal Vesco had further described proselytism as “a poison because it implies considering the other person’s religion to be false.” Lest this be a simple misunderstanding, Cardinal Vesco doubled down, 

Yes, I believe that the believers of the three monotheistic religions have better things to do than to seek to convert one another. Rather, they should accept that there is a measure of what they cannot know about the faith of the other, and respect one another in their respective faiths. Our world needs believers who are deeply rooted in their own faith and who recognize one another as brothers and sisters in our one sacred humanity.

Curiously, there seems to be a violent allergy, including among Catholics, to the word “convert.” To convert, in the eyes of the trembling many, means “to proselytize.” And to proselytize conjures up images of seething crusaders, hand-rubbing inquisitors, and sandwich-board sporting the-end-is-nearists. 

But this is ridiculous. 

Show me the aggressive, brow-beating Catholic proselytizer. Please. Because no such thing exists in the wild anymore. As a former Lutheran who was once looking for reasons not to like Catholics, I never met one. The fearsome proselytizer is a tired trope. It is a bogeyman of bygone Christendom trotted out whenever the season demands in order to spook away any honest attempt to win someone over to the Catholic faith. 

Many Catholics these days are so fearful of being deemed overcompensating proselytizers that they dreadfully undercompensate to the point where they remain, like Peter in the garden, mute about their faith. For fear of stepping on another’s toes, we trade in enlightened relativism, speak the milquetoast language of “humanity,” and worship at the altar of inoffensiveness. C. S. Lewis would castigate this spineless middle ground, saying, “Christianity, if false, is of no importance, and if true, of infinite importance. The only thing it cannot be is moderately important.” And in his captivating book, The Tyranny of Guilt, French essayist Pascal Bruckner warns of the wreckage that remains from such waywardness of principle born out of self-doubt and self-flagellation,

The critical spirit rises up against itself and consumes its form. But instead of coming out of this process greater and purified, it devours itself in a kind of self-cannibalism and takes a morose pleasure in annihilating itself. Hyper-criticism eventuates in self-hatred, leaving behind it only ruins. 

A Catholic faith void of its evangelizing mission is desperately in crisis. It holds a truth, but is too shy to share it. It believes in heaven, but only one that meets your satisfaction. It subscribes to rules but not the kind that will hurt your feelings. Before long, such a faith is a rudderless ship tossed about by the waves of modern whims and buttoned-down ideologies. Such a faith is a club bled white of dogma, a clique unbothered by tradition, a movement freed from the Gospel, a church without Christ. Desacralized. Disincarnate. And we become, as Georges Bernanos might describe, “horrible undeveloped monsters, the stumps of men.” If we hold a sacred truth—but not so sacred and not so true that we are galvanized to share it—then it is little more than a heart-warming story and quaint cultural symbol. But if it is only a symbol, then, to borrow from Flannery O’Connor, “to hell with it.”

That’s not my Catholic Church.

Now let me set the record straight. To convert—to effectively evangelize—is not to coerce or cudgel, browbeat or badger someone into belief. That is impossible. It is a contradiction in terms. There is no such thing as compelled belief. To subscribe to a faith is to have freely assented to it. 

Furthermore, evangelizing is not loud or condescending, caustic or judgmental. It is born of prudence. To convert someone means that you see them as a dignified child of God worthy of love and respect. It means that you acknowledge that they have free will and, as such, have the option to simply walk away. And finally, it means that the truth is, in fact, the truth and it matters enough and you love someone enough to put yourself in the uncomfortable position of telling them about it. Perhaps this is best illustrated in a quote attributed (though likely apocryphal) to St. Thomas Aquinas, “To convert somebody, go and take them by the hand and guide them.” To evangelize and convert is an act of deep love and earnest intentionality. 

When Andrew brought Simon Peter to Jesus, Peter changed. When Phillip told Bartholomew (Nathaniel) to “Come and see,” Bartholomew was transformed. When Ananias accompanied the archenemy Paul deep into his faith, Paul was remade. When Monica prayed (and modeled Christian charity) for seventeen years on behalf of her wayward son, Augustine was converted. When Fr. John O’Connor and Hilaire Belloc befriended G. K. Chesterton, he was revolutionized. 

“I believe,” Cardinal Vesco insisted, “that the believers of the three monotheistic religions have better things to do than to seek to convert one another.” Perhaps if we were to follow the cardinal’s philosophy, everything would work out.

Perhaps.
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

But then, perhaps, we wouldn’t have the rock of the Church, two incomparable missionary evangelists (who also made a living converting people), a Doctor of the Church, and one of the greatest Catholic apologists of the age. All were converted because someone decided that, out of love and intentionality, they wanted to take them by the hand and guide them. 

Finally, I am a convert. And if it wasn’t for the love of my wife, investment of my best friend, indulgence of countless priests, insight of numberless novelists and apologists, and the sublime grace of God—all wanting me to become Catholic yet loving me in my freedom—I never would have made the greatest decision of my life. 

Recognize the dignity of others. Respect their free will. And love the truth and the call to share it. 

Yes, Cardinal Vesco, out of love, out of hope, out of supreme interest in willing the good of the other, we are called to convert the world. 

Let’s take others by the hand and guide them.

It’s a problem we’ll address this week on The Land and the Book. Plus, we’ll have all the headlines from the Middle East—and some intriguing listener Bible questions.
